utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Cvijetic, Tatjana Savic, and Eugene O'Sullivan for the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no housekeeping matters, may the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Cvijetic continues his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, yesterday we began to discuss your visit to the Doboj CSB, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with another topic that has to do with Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 1D356.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is tab 12. I apologise, but could I ask the usher to hand the binder to the witness. Let me just check if we can see the document on the screen, because I can't see it there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please open the binder at tab 12. Have you seen it, this criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do read the report and then I'll ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: While reviewing criminal reports at the Doboj CSB, did you see this one? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I'm reading it and I see the date, the 1st of August, and the rest, then, yeah, I remember that this body was found in a freezer. Yes, I remember this detail. This criminal report was registered and submitted to the prosecutor's office. The investigative magistrate was present at the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This report is dated 1 August. As far as I remember, you were there after the criminal report had been submitted?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our visit was on the 25th of August. That's when we visited the Doboj CSB. And the offence was committed before and registered. An on-site investigation was made, and the report was submitted to the public prosecutor's office, as can be seen by the report itself. I remember. This is one of the reports that we saw and discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll show you another from the period before your arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D357.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read the report, please, so it may jog your memory, and then I'll ask you about it. The tab number is 13. I hope you found it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'm reading the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, try to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you remember. But very briefly tell us if you saw this report.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, and we discussed this report when we were in Doboj. I remember since the tool used in the commission of the offence was a knife, and I used -- I took a sheet of paper and put down the place and time of commission as well as the tool used. That's why I remember. An on-site investigation was made and the report was submitted to the prosecutor's office. This is the second report of about a dozen. I'm not sure how many were against known and how many against unknown perpetrators, but I seem to remember the last name of the person -- last names of the persons mentioned here. The criminal reports entered in the log also included this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I only wanted to check whether these are the reports that you reviewed at the time. They are already exhibits, so no need to comment on them much. You mentioned unknown perpetrators. Was there a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator where the victim was a Serb, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about it. I don't remember how many reports were against known perpetrators. There was one criminal report against a Serb perpetrator and the victim was also a Serb. They were from the same village and their names were similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, but my question was whether there was a report where a Serb was the victim and the perpetrator unknown.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some such reports. But the procedure was the same whenever the perpetrator of a murder was unknown. The offence was registered --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do explain what you said, the procedure was the same when there was an unknown perpetrator; what exactly do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there was an unknown perpetrator, the procedure was the same regardless of the identity of the victim. The identity or the ethnic affiliation of the victim didn't matter to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll show you another criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's from the 65 ter list. 388D1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, please read this and pay attention to the date the offence was committed.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question is the same as about the previous two: Is this a case of the type we discussed, an unknown perpetrator and a Serb victim? Can you draw that conclusion based on the names halfway through the text? Take a look at the names of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Sorry. I think we can all read this and see what it says, but is it the case that the witness has seen this before, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he can't have seen this criminal report when he was there. But my question was the same because I want to point out once more that the procedure was identical regardless of who the victim was. I'm not going to tender this criminal report because he hasn't seen it, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let me comment. I wanted to say with regard to the date, 10 November, we were there on 25 August and clearly we couldn't have seen this, but the procedure and the way of going about it were the same. The reports that were registered before the 25th and -- which we analysed, it's the same as here. The victims were Serbs but the procedure was the same regardless of who the victim was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the essence of my question. Since you haven't seen this document before, I'm not going to tender it. Mr. Orasanin, do you know how long you stayed at Doboj? When did your visit finish?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we spent the night at a hotel. It may have been an old people's home which was turned into a hotel. On the following day we visited the Banja Luka CSB, so it means that we stayed in Doboj two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This was going to be my next question, where did you move on to, but you've already said that you moved on to Banja Luka. Tell us, then, how long you stayed in Banja Luka or when you actually arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, having spent the night in Doboj, we set off for Banja Luka. As far as I remember, we went by way of Stanari. That was a route that we were able to take at the time, and we visited the Banja Luka CSB. That was our following visit to an organisational unit. It was the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you remember who came to meet you there? Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be honest about it, when we arrived at the CSB in Banja Luka, I called at a colleague, Vladimir Tutus, and I spoke to him. And I believe that Nikola Milanovic and Ostoja went to see the deputy chief of the centre or possibly the chief himself. I think the deputy chief was Bulic and they spoke to him. But since I knew Vladimir Tutus, he was my generation at school, I called on him and I wanted to see the logs and hear what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Since you split, I'll ask you what you inspected in your line of work when you arrived in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did the same there as we had done pursuant to our instructions. We reviewed the crimes log-book, what the SJBs do when they receive criminal complaints, whether they are submitted to the prosecutor's office, whether the prosecutors get involved. And as far as I remember, the logs were in order. They were kept in accordance with the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What did you find there with regard to the processing of criminal offences? Did you inspect that, and what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the same as in Doboj: criminal reports were submitted to the prosecutor's office, they were registered, and they engaged in some operative activities. But I don't remember how many they had. They had a certain number of operatives. I contacted one inspector; his name was Jevic, Drago Jevic. He was one of the inspectors there at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So what would be your assessment of the situation there with regard to your line of work?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did the same thing as in Doboj. We checked if criminal reports were entered into the logs and whether they were acting in accordance with the instructions about crime prevention and detection. I remember that there was a lot of activity there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And what about your colleagues who went with you, did they do the same thing you did?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had the same mission, the same task. We were a team that was sent on behalf of the Crime Prevention Administration, so we shared the same task. We were sent to see whether regulations were being applied, primarily the instruction on the prevention and detection of crimes. That was our task and that was their task as well. I believe that Nikola Milanovic and I looked at some criminal report that had been registered there. However, if I were to look at the reports, I might be able to remember them. But anything that happened before the 26th and 27th of August when we arrived, so I'm talking about those reports, the reports that had been filed before those dates and were processed by the crime prevention services in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That would have been my next question. When you arrived there, had some of the cases already been processed and submitted to the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember them. If you were to show me some of those reports, I would be able to remember them just as I did with those from Doboj, when I remembered some three or four criminal reports that were filed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you finished your visit to Banja Luka, where did you go next? Which route did you take, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took the same way back, Stanari-Doboj-Modrica. However, we had received intelligence that the commander or the deputy commander of the police station in Doboj had been wounded at Samac and that's why we stopped to visit him, but just for a brief period, for half an hour. We actually went to his house, visited him, and then we proceeded towards Brcko and Bijeljina. And I know that later on when we arrived in Bijeljina and when we looked at the situation there, some new activities were planned in order to prepare some other things and to find resources for the implementation of all the tasks that we had been engaged in Doboj and Samac and so on and so forth. That was our plan for later. And some people were engaged after the 29th or 30th of August to implement that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That would have been my next question precisely. Maybe you can tell us also whether what you had observed on the ground, should that have been controlled, should some measures have been undertaken where you noticed weaknesses? You already said that there were plans, but if you want to add something to that, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we visited Doboj and Banja Luka, and since we were affiliated with the same administration and we were very cautious when it came to competences and authorities, at least I myself did not want to interfere with other people's authorities, and we noticed that in Doboj there were problems with manning the reserve police force and other problems, so when we returned to Bijeljina, we had a proposal that there should be a mixed team represented by the police administration, by inspectors who would be more familiar with that part of the job. And I believe that later on a mixed team was indeed set up involving uniformed police and police from the Administration for Crime Prevention. We thought that it would be better if such a team was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So did such a team indeed go to Doboj after you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember the date. I don't remember whether that was perhaps 10 or 15 days later. In any case, I remember that a person was sent on behalf of the police administration. I believe that that was the assistant minister and Goran Macar on behalf of the crime prevention police, Radenko Vujicic perhaps, Cedo Tosic also, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can't remember any other details, never mind. Let me ask you this: During that subsequent visit, were they supposed to also visit Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that was planned. We were there only for perhaps half an hour. There were some problems there, and they were supposed to go there and fix those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to your next visit, tell me something about your method of work. When you, for example, returned from a visit of that kind, how did you report to your superior administration and your superiors as to what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our obligation to file a report on our work, which encompassed everything that we did pursuant to rules and regulations dealing with such instructive visit. And the terminology we used was "visit" to police stations and crime prevention departments, the reason being that there were no conditions in place in order to carry out a complete supervision. Pursuant to the prevalent laws, such a complete supervision would have encompassed a lot more than we had time for. We did not have time for a thorough inspection. It would have taken at least five or six days to carry out such a thorough inspection, and that's why we filed a report on visits to police stations or tours of the police stations. As per rules, it should have been reports on the instructive supervision of the police stations. The term itself implies a lot more obligations, a lot more things than we actually did, that's why we used a different terminology in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now this -- after your visits, were there supposed to be instructive supervisions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that this terminology was subsequently used once the instruction on instructive supervision was drafted, but that was later. In 1992, unfortunately regulations were lacking. It was very early days, so the administrations in the ministry were working on drafting proposals for such future instructions, and it was the minister who was supposed to issue such instructions pursuant to the Law on State Administration. He was the one who issued decisions, instructions, and regulations. At that time, during the time, the period of transition, some of the police stations were in the eastern part and were not encompassed by the police administration and the ministry, and that's why there was a gap, a shortage of regulations and rules. I believe that rules and regulations were finally issued in late 1992, or, rather, I think that there was a rule on internal organisation that was in the pipeline. I don't know when it was actually issued. Hence all the shortcomings. And that's why we called our visits "visit," although such things did not exist in the rules. It was a huge responsibility. It would have been a huge responsibility if we had called it an inspection supervision, since it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since you touched upon the topic on regulations on internal organisation yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, where are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm dealing with the things that the witness did on behalf of the Crime Prevention Administration. I will be dealing with my -- with his next visit, and my next question will pursue the team that he has just touched upon. I want to ask him whether before the regulations were issued did the minister take any steps to remove all those who did not comply with the regulations from the Ministry of the Interior; did he do that even before regulations were issued. And my next topic, the next thing that I'm going to pursue, is his next visit, his next inspection. That's how I've planned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I believe the Chamber has been -- has been receiving a lot of evidence about the rules and the procedures that applied to these inspections, and I don't think that there's any disagreement about it either from the Prosecution side. So this seems to be a very dry path to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly accept, and we always have, that the inspections took place. What happened as a result of the inspections is another matter. But certainly inspections took place, and we've got reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So there you have it, Mr. Cvijetic. Can I suggest that you proceed straight to the results of these inspections and the steps that the minister took in response to those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just make an observation. In relation to the transcript on page 11, line 24, in that line you'll see a sentence begins with the words "all those such things," and I believe the interpreter said "although such things."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Please proceed, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the minister to do something, he has to receive report from the ground. For example, the next visit by the team that went --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No speeches, thank you. Not while the witness is listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to answer Judge Harhoff's remark and answer his question. Please don't interrupt me while I'm doing that. I am explaining why I want to deal with the next issue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. But the witness, if he doesn't -- I don't know whether he speaks English or not, should take his headphones off while you explain, if he doesn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, are you -- do you speak English? Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, he also needs to turn off the microphone because otherwise he gets the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we hope that you will be able to address us in this matter in English. If that is not an option --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, it's not an option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If this is not the case, then we should ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But before we go on with this, returning to the intervention that Judge Harhoff made earlier and Ms. Korner's response, there is no issue, Mr. Cvijetic, as to whether these reports were done, so I'm at a loss as to why you still consider it necessary to pursue the fact of these reports having gone up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's a report which hasn't been admitted and we want to tender it because it is in our interest, and that report is about the last visit. I don't know why I should be prevented from tendering it. And those visits that the witness is talking about actually illustrate the method of work that was applied by the Crime Prevention Administration and the ministry. Even after such short visits high-quality instructive inspections were prepared pursuant to the minister's decisions and orders, and once the minister received reports, the minister would react with documents that have already been admitted. I'm just trying to lay the foundation as to what preceded and what the minister learned about what was going on on the ground, what was the organisation on the ground, what the weaknesses were, and how he reacted. I'm just trying to give you the logical course of events in practical terms from the visit to the decisions by the minister. In other words, this visit -- this witness participated in another visit. I would like him to tell us something about it, and I would like to tender a report from that visit that has still not been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic, for your account. But you see, if you look at the clock, it has taken you 45 minutes to get here to the question of whether or not this witness filed a report after his inspections and whether he submitted this report to the minister. I really don't find all the background that you have taken the witness to explain to be very useful to the Chamber because we know that these inspections took place and the Prosecution agrees and stipulates to the fact that they did take place. So this is an example, Mr. Cvijetic, of the way we would like you to proceed when we continue, namely to get straight to the point, and not seek to go through every piece of evidence which we really don't need in the end. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the report of the visits to the following four municipalities that Mr. Orasanin with his team of inspectors went to isn't anything you need, then I can drop the remaining examination on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think you should actually drop them because what the Chamber needs in terms of evidence is proof of the information that was passed from this witness up to the ministry and to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's what we've been discussing all the time, Your Honour. This is the official way of receiving information on the part of the minister. And so if that is not relevant, I don't know how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the criminal reports that you have brought to the witness this morning are of no significance in respect of what this witness reported up to the minister after his inspections. We know that the criminal reports were made in the CSBs and in the SJBs, and the Prosecution agrees to it. We know that the inspections took place, and the Prosecution agrees to that as well. Now, from this point on, the crucial element is: What was the results of these inspections, did the inspectors file reports up to the minister, and what was the contents of these reports; and secondly, did the minister ever receive the reports. In terms of the charges in the indictment, this is really the evidence that we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all this you're looking for you can hear from this witness and see in these documents. This is the very thing. What follows, and I can say for the sake of reference, is 65 ter 33D1 in relation to which I want to discuss the Visegrad municipality, which is covered by the indictment. If do you not care to hear that, we will not deal about it, but that was going to be next. It's a written report of the visit conducted. This is what you are looking for, a written report about the situation in these stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Cvijetic, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. 65 ter 33D1 is a report of inspection to the minister, as I understand it; right? Or to the ministry; right? So that's the kind of evidence we are indeed looking for, and you should certainly not drop that one. If it's related to municipalities in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What is the tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That would be tab number - where is it? - 32, if I'm not wrong. Is that right, Mr. Cvijetic, tab number 32?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, it's tab 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's a criminal report once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. 65 ter 33D1 is under tab 29, and it's a report on the visit to Foca, Cajnice, Rudo, and Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, I'm mixing up the tab numbers. It's indeed 29 and it's indeed the report on inspection. So that one, if that's a report of this witness to go to the ministry, you should proceed and ask the witness about it, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cvijetic, now that you -- it's been -- now that we understand where we're going, could the usher please escort the witness back in. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just ask where this document comes from? The one you're going to be showing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is best to ask the witness that. Oh, yes, and we got it from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to go through any more questions like with Mr. Bjelosevic. If I could be given, please, a list of anything that is in this binder which comes from this witness, please, just to save time asking each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do I take it, Mr. Cvijetic, that your silence should be interpreted as an affirmative response to Ms. Korner's request?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are checking, Your Honours. I know that we received this report from him. We may have received some other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not expecting Mr. Cvijetic -- I'm not expecting an immediate answer from Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two documents, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they are announced already. But the witness will explain, but I believe we only received two documents from him. That is not so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin - let us just wait for the English translation - please open the binder at tab 29. Take a look, sir. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We have to explain yet how the Defence came by this document. Or let me ask you straightaway: Did you give it to us?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had this report on me, but I didn't have it when I was interviewed by the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orasanin, during this inspection, you visited the SJBs of Foca, Cajnice, Rudo, and Visegrad, so just tell us to which CSB do these SJBs belong?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 when we were there in early September, the SJBs of Foca, Cajnice, Rudo, and Visegrad belonged to the Trebinje CSB. And if necessary, I can also say what the pre-war organisation was. Foca belonged to Gorazde and so did Cajnice. I'm not sure about Rudo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that a group of SJBs that were left without their CSB once the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same case as with the SJBs along the Drina. They belonged to Gorazde. And as far as the crime prevention service is concerned, they were left hanging. Later they were -- they were placed under the authority of a CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It wasn't recorded which CSB.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one of Trebinje in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, please turn the page and find the Visegrad SJB. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Halfway through there is a statement that the prosecutor's office and the court have not started operating. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may explain, it was the same as in Rudo, Visegrad, and Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read the final section. You also propose measures to be taken to improve the situation. Please read that part.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is our proposal and a comment that more attention should be given to these SJBs. The Trebinje CSB visits these stations rarely, that is, they aren't covered. And there's also a statement about the prosecutor's office and the court. So our proposal was to provide them technical assistance or professional assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did the ministry or your administration react to improve the situation? Did anybody go there later?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, after our stay there was discussion in our administration that Nikola Milanovic, I think, and Sinisa Karan should go there after some time once the shortcomings are rectified. The following visit was planned and the ones to go there were Sinisa Karan and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the second person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Apart from Sinisa Karan, who was to go there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Nikola Milanovic to go there on behalf of the Crime Prevention Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll show you the following document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but first I seek to tender this document because this is a report signed by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D571, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another document also dealing with Visegrad. P633 is its number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the second page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it could easily be page 3. In the English version it's the last paragraph on this page. And in the Serbian version I've already told you it's on page 2, paragraph 3, starting with the words "from the early days, the Visegrad Public Security Station has functioned."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the third paragraph. We can all read, can't we?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this gives an overview of the situation in the public security station, a lack of staff, and it says that there were only five professional police officers there. This is what the report is about. It highlights the shortage of the professional police staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could all read that, but I would like to ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, "we could all read that," you say, but we can't. It's probably the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, yes, it does go on to the following page. That's why you actually couldn't read it. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, what you have just told us, that there were only five active police officers, but I'm interested in the introductory part where it says that the leadership of that police station had the War Presidency of Visegrad; this is something I wanted to ask you about: Did you know about that when you arrived in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the police stations in the eastern part were appointed by the War Presidency. That was the case in Skelani and Visegrad. The local government, or, rather, the War Presidency appointed a commander and a deputy commander, and that was not a problem only in Visegrad but also in all the other police stations that I mentioned yesterday, Zvornik, Visegrad, Skelani, and that was that the War Presidency appointed the leadership staff in the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version we will see that on the previous page where the War Presidency is mentioned. Can we go to the previous page for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. We are looking for page 3 in English to be displayed in e-court. The last paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You've already answered my question about the War Presidency. Could you please move on to the following page, page 3 in the Serbian version, and you will see a reference to the reserve police force in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously we will have to see what page this is on in the English version. I believe it's on page 4 in e-court in the English version. It will be the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a moment to read the paragraph which in the English version goes on to the following page. It's a lengthy paragraph. I will give you a moment to read that paragraph in the Serbian version of the document and then I'll have questions for you. Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the first part it says that there were 150 reserve policemen to begin with. I'm not interested in what it says, but what I would like to know is whether you were instructed to reduce the number of police officers, reserve policemen, where there were too many?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this was a prevalent problem in 1992. This was an instruction or an order which I remember, it was issued by the minister, for the reserve police strength to be reduced in compliance with the organisation and to remove those that did not comply with the requirements. And here you can see that the number was reduced from 150 to 40 reserve policemen. There's reference to some crimes and difficulties in preventing crimes in the territory of the Visegrad Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Wait, let's look at the last part where paramilitary formations are mentioned and also the problems that they were causing. The question is -- the question is very specific: Were you informed about this problem once you inspected the police station in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Nikola Milanovic spoke to Perisic. I personally didn't. That is why he planned a subsequent visit to the police station in Foca, because there was a problem with those groups that prevented the police from doing their work. They looted property, they broke in apartments. My colleague spoke to the chief, and my colleague also was the one who planned a subsequent visit after our return. I know all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orasanin, could you please tell us which route you took in order to visit those four police stations? How many kilometres did you do on your visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that it was a problem, the problem with regard to our stay and the conditions of our stay. The total distance was over 500 kilometres from the moment we departed from either Bijeljina or Pale. In order to reach Visegrad and Foca, you have to do over 500 kilometres. If you wanted to take a short cut via Sarajevo to Pale to Foca, it would have been 80 kilometres. We had to cross the territory of the present three states. We had to go to Serbia along the right bank of the Drina River, across Tara Mountain, and then we had to go to the Republic of Montenegro via Pljevlja along some scenic macadam roads barely passable. We used such roads, and that's why we visited Cajnice and Rudo as well, because they were on our route. We took some adjacent auxiliary routes to all those places. We encountered some problems and difficulties on our way. We even encountered some threats, but it's neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you use the same route to go to the Security Services Centre in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same, there's no other road. You had to go from Bijeljina via Zvornik, then you have to cross to a different state, and then along the left river bank, cross Bajina Basta, Tara, you have to cross the border to Montenegro, and then arrive in the territory of Pljevlja. And then you take a right turn towards Foca or you go via Trebinje; in other words, you could have continued through Montenegro via Puzine to arrive in Trebinje. You had to cross almost entire Montenegro to get to Trebinje because that was the only safe road at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was it possible to take the shortest possible way? When did that road become passable?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was in 1993, but I'm not sure. I'm talking about the road leading from Sarajevo to Trnovo and then on to Karanovac and Foca and then Gacko, Bilice, Trebinje. That is the road. I believe that it became passable in mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orasanin, we have seen that you took four different routes for your visits. I'm not sure that there were four. Could you tell us how many such visits and trips did you take while you worked in the Crime Prevention Administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four visits. One was a visit to the area of Podrinje, including Skelani, Brcko, Zvornik, Bijeljina, Vogosca, and Ilijas. And then another one to Doboj and Banja Luka. And the fourth visit was along the route that I've just described. The first visit was to Foca, and then on return we visited Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice. That was the fourth visit that we undertook.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did your colleagues from the administration cover any other areas that you yourself did not visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, one team of inspectors did visit, or, rather, revisit Samac and Doboj. That was probably sometime in September, October. Maybe they even went twice. They visited Brcko, and I believe that a team was sent to the area of Trebinje as well. And there was also a plan in place to pay another visit to Visegrad. One team was to be sent to visit Visegrad and Foca, but I can't remember. I left the Crime Prevention Administration, so I'm not familiar with any of the detail. I'm sure that a team did go just as I have just said, that they went to Doboj and Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Slow down a little. It is not clear from the transcript that there were four visits. It seems that all those stations were visited on one visit. Can you do it to make a clear separation between those visits?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first visit was to Zvornik, Skelani, Foca, Brcko, and Bijeljina. That was the first visit. The second visit was to Vogosca and Ilijas. The third visit was to Doboj and Banja Luka and stopping in Samac. And the fourth and last visit was to Foca, Rudo, Cajnice, and Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, you said that you visited Foca the first time around and you omitted Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one was Zvornik, Skelani, Brcko, and Bijeljina. That was the first visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So no Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No Foca. We visited Foca in September, not earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note the time. I'm about to move on to the topic that I've already announced and that is the drafting of some regulations by the Ministry of the Interior, and this witness participated in the drafting of those proposals. And this is a completely separate topic from the topic of visits, that's why I think it would be a good idea to take a break now and then after the break I would be prepared to move on to that next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well, so we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, during any stage of the proceedings or the procedure, did you participate in drafting some legal regulations that were later signed by the minister and passed by the minister?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This had to do with the Administration for Crime Prevention and specifically about war crimes and deposits made, registrations and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I called it, because these documents are signed and adopted by the minister. But what I wanted to know was how such a document would reach the minister and how that text of that document would be drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to show you two documents. First the exhibit which is Exhibit 1D538, tab 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This dispatch -- we see in this dispatch the minister of the interior is urging other people to take action pursuant to a document.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I can see the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And mention is made there that anyone who should fail to take the measures as required would be called to duty. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is this the area that you mentioned earlier that you were involved in drafting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The minister is requesting here that certain actions have to be taken that relate to deposits made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you now tell us, please, what is the purpose of registering deposits in a SJB, in a public security station? And you will tell us where that was done.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the rules on registering deposits, each public security station has the duty to have a log-book of deposits, and the rules actually regulate this issue, how items are to be handled. And specifically it describes the items that are involved or related to crime proceedings. So once a criminal report is submitted to the prosecution, the competent prosecutor's office, then those items are deposited, but in fact those deposited items are now within the jurisdiction of the court. So the public security stations have to keep track and have a log-book of such deposits. And here we see that the minister is requesting to be informed on the deposits that had been made and whether they have been done in a proper way as required by the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason I'm asking you about this is this: Was there any -- were there any reports that there were abuses of these items that had been deposited? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall any specific case, but I assume that this dispatch actually is the result of such possible reports that in some public security stations there were some abuses or that the procedure for registering deposited items was not properly enforced. And that's quite clear. But then there are also other deposits that have to do with reserve goods, and that would be guided and regulated by another set of rules, and this specific dispatch is actually something that reflects that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will show you another document that was sent by the minister, 1D64, since you mentioned the reserves, strategic reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you please read this order issued by the minister and then we will briefly comment on it. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it clear?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please now just answer my question: Does this order relate to the other type of items and the other type of registered deposits?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this has do with commodity reserves. And as far as I can recall, this was done at the level of the municipality by the authorities. There was a commission, I believe, that would compile such items. But here we see that those items that were subject to a criminal investigation, that they should be handled by the public security stations, whereas the items that were under the law within the competence of the commodity reserves, that they should be handed over to the commodity reserves organs. So here it is also said that if anyone should not abide by these instructions, that they would be punished. In other words, abuses would be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to show you the instructions on keeping a log of reserves, and that would be -- or rather, of keeping a log of all deposits, and that would be under 65 ter -- that's 65 ter 117D1. Tab 32. Let's just wait for the English version to come up and then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, we will just take a brief look at the first page. This is the cover letter sent by the chief of the Security Services Centre, Krsto Savic. The Security Services Centre in Trebinje. And he is forwarding and distributing this document within his Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like us to see page 2, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this. Is this a document which was drafted among others by you, or, rather, you took part in the drafting of this document, can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, these are instructions on how to store items, and we actually prepared a draft version as the public security station but this document was in fact done by the legal services. However, the items in these instructions are the ones that we proposed. We had a typed-written version because we didn't -- we just had a typewriter, we didn't have any other type of device. But the subject matter and the contents of these instructions are the same, and this is -- these instructions were the ones that were adopted and passed by the minister after they have been given the proper legal form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted to show how such documents were sent to the minister and how they were forwarded to the minister for signing, for his signature. Now, I do also have that typewritten form, but I would just like it to show it briefly to you, that's 1D06, so that you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 1D065505.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I would like to show it to you so that you can just confirm for us whether that is the original document that you had typewritten. And that's under tab 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can keep the same English version because the documents are identical, and we do not actually have a translation of the typewritten document. So can we just keep them as they are on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Orasanin, please take a look at this document and tell us whether you recognise your own work, as it were, if I may put it that way. And do you recognise the tripe writer that was used to type it up? You can see it on the left-hand side, please take a look. You also have a hard copy, and that's under tab -- oh, my apologies. I will give it to you in the moment. It's not in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, but you will also get the original document, the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... what number is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was announced. It was under number 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at the hard copy. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please tell us whether that's the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I know that this typewriter would also sometimes go and type in a slanted way. You can see it in the signature that it's not parallel to the other lines because it was a tiny little machine, a Bizer typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you were the agency that proposed such a document. Now, what was the next step?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the next step was this would go to the legal administration and they would give it proper legal form and then it would be forwarded by them to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, I will touch upon another document where you were involved in its drafting, at least as far as the text was concerned. So could we see 1D63 now. That's tab 35. My apologies, I haven't said it? Do you have it before you? That's tab 35? Yes, that's the one. Now please take a look at the cover letter first before you look at the form. Here we see that the form or questionnaire is being forwarded, and you can see from the first paragraph that it's a form which would be used to enter information regarding war crimes. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And do you see there that it also says that it should be entered regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator against whom the report, criminal reports, have been submitted? Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but this was also worked on and further expanded at the minister's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as far as I can recall, we took this document with us when we went to the field. We didn't wait for this to be officially forwarded. We took it with us when we went in the field, and it did have to do with war crimes. And it's true that -- well, at that time no one even considered the aspect of ethnicity. That was not something that was taken into account at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see page 2 so that we can take a look at that questionnaire, or form. That's the next page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, this form has a certain name. It says, in the title, "Form RZ." Could you please tell us what "RZ" stands for in our language?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this form was type written in the Cyrillic script, and RZ stands for war crimes, "ratni zlocin." In other words, victims of war crimes, that's what RZ indicates. In other words, regardless of the ethnicity of the victim, all information was captured in this general form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, was there another form -- was there a special form that was to be used in the cases where Serbs were the victims?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was a different type of form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What kind of designation did it have?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: R1. So this is "ratni zlocin," war crimes, and general. In other words, of general aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, but in your response you said "R1." Would it be, in fact, "RZ1"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. RZ1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These forms and the instructions to register war crimes, did you carry them with you to the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were duty-bound to submit these forms and enter information in them, and they would be forwarded to the analyses department.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Orasanin, I'll show a document now, 1D065506 or 920D1. Tab 38, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we were informed by the translation service that the English translation of this document is due any minute. It was only disclosed on Thursday. Therefore, I suggest that the witness read out the contents of this dispatch from Minister Stanisic or that I move on to my last topic and then we can get back to this document once the translation has arrived. This dispatch is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask the witness now whether he knows this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since he knows this dispatch, we would like to tender it. But I ask the Trial Chamber how I should go about it and have it done by the end of today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but I haven't the faintest idea what it says. So we can have the witness read it out and then I'll see, but at the moment this is not something I know whether I can agree to or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I, too, thought of having him read it out, but then we would still have to return to it once we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So perhaps Mr. Cvijetic's alternative of moving on to something else then returning to that is the better course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, I wanted to discuss this with you at the end, but we are still waiting for the English translation and then we'll see what we'll do next. When you spoke about the regulations on internal organisation, you said that a condition for somebody to be issued a final appointment as a MUP employee was to meet the requirements of the regulations. You said that it was not in force in 1992 and that everybody only got temporary appointments. Did the minister intervene by issuing orders to alleviate the situation in the ministry at least somewhat and remove those who did not meet the legal conditions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I've resisted this morning objecting to leading questions, but that one is really atrocious. The proper question is, What did the minister do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree that the question is as leading as that, Your Honours. And the question was, Did the minister take any steps to alleviate the situation. I believe -- well, this is the proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We agree with Ms. Korner here, Mr. Cvijetic. The question could have been differently put.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How did the minister alleviate the situation until the regulations entered into force?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- or, rather, I remember an order or a dispatch from 1992 which was sent out to the SJBs, or the CSBs and then forwarded to the SJBs, to review the staffing level of the organisational units, that the number of staff should be reduced and adapted to the organisational structure, and that the -- those members of the police should be removed who did not meet the conditions. And those were both the general and the special conditions under both the labour law and the Law on Internal Affairs which gives special powers to police staff based on checks that are conducted to find out whether they are suitable for police work, and those members were from public security. They have special powers and can exercise police powers. Another group consists of those who do not belong to this sector, that is, those who work in the administration and legal department. The latter should be removed and placed at the disposal of the military. Those who are responsible for any wrong-doing should be subject to disciplinary action but only if they are proper police staff, because only as such are they liable to disciplinary proceedings. It was also proposed that they be given temporary appointments which entail what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was the purpose of these orders achieved?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Except in some stations. I don't remember whether Doboj carried out what they were duty-bound to do. As far as the reserve police force is concerned, I said yesterday that they were -- there were shortcomings or, rather, resistance to the minister's order which was very clear. I remember Doboj. I can't remember whether there was anything like that in other municipalities or SJBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know anything about the operation against paramilitaries in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with these details because I was to be the duty officer in the crime prevention service of the MUP. The operation was prepared earlier because there was intelligence about the presence of paramilitaries. It was my duty to be on duty shift and follow the activities of the Crime Prevention Department, whatever was happening in the field. But other people went out to implement it, to carry it out. As far as I know, a special unit also took part. But we had to wait a bit for it all to be organised because we lacked some equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about that operation because you weren't in the field to take part directly. Let me just ask you what the role of inspectors from the Crime Prevention Administration in such an operation was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't take direct part. But the role of a crime prevention inspector was to assist the local inspectors to carry it out. I know that Nikola Milanovic, I think, took part, and so did Ostoja Minic. The administration was to draft an operative plan for the implementation of the operation, but there was also the police administration who had their plan, and they had their materiel and technical equipment. Our plan that we worked out at the Crime Prevention Administration became an annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What exactly was envisaged by that plan?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interviewing of persons, the arresting of persons, any investigative activities, given the approval of the investigative magistrate and the prosecutor, and anything else that the police has a right to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you personally to take part in this operation that we can call Foca now, and if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time. I can't remember everything. After the operation, and it was all in August, all these planned activities of the MUP, I was convinced that the operation had been carried out without my participation because I was transferred to another position. We were drafting an operative plan for going to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But my question was only: Did you have the opportunity to see an order about the execution of such an operation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I was convinced that it had indeed taken place. I remember that I drafted the operative plan and the order was clear. There was something in that order that I remember. There was the order to arrest those paramilitaries that were called terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt and object. At the moment Your Honours, as it were, adjourned your ruling on this matter. I think we need an explanation of how this is relevant, as Foca is not within the indictment nor have Your Honours heard anything about the events in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- when Ms. Korner adumbrated this matter yesterday, you indicated that you only intended to touch on Foca. The Chamber, as Ms. Korner has rightly said, never ruled on her objection, and it seems that the time has come for you to formulate a response that would enable the Chamber to rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm afraid it would have to be in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, that struck me as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, from time to time, these procedural matters arise which are best taken out of the hearing of the witness, so again I would ask the usher to escort you from the room for the time being, while we resolve this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I said yesterday, I will not deal with the events in Foca. I will deal with the events at Pale and Minister Stanisic's order to carry out that operation. Why? I will deal with the intention of Minister Stanisic, and it is relevant for his responsibility under the indictment. His intention to eradicate negative occurrences in the RS. We want to point out that this was not a single operation or two sporadic operations but a sequence of continuous operations as soon as the conditions were met, from Brcko to Bijeljina to Zvornik to Foca. In other words, I am dealing with the mens rea of Mico Stanisic and his persistence in coping with these occurrences, and it can be seen in the order to launch the operation in Foca. This witness was saying that he personally read the order and, based on that, drafted an operative plan of action for the crime prevention service to carry out the tasks that Mr. Stanisic had given them. Tasks were also assigned to anybody else involved in that operation, that is, the special unit of the police, the police administration, and others. We are exclusively dealing with Pale and Minister Stanisic's order as well as the operative plan for such an operation. We will not go to Foca. And apart from that, the operation was never conducted. I wish to remind the Trial Chamber that Witness Dragan Andan gave evidence about that operation and evidence was introduced through him about who was meant to participate, with what, and so on, and it may be interesting and relevant for the Trial Chamber to hear evidence about that. We now have a witness who read the order, and I believe that it is very relevant to see it because it shows to what extent Minister Stanisic persevered in the carrying out of such operations. This is what I would like to show.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is -- I'd have to check on the evidence of Mr. Andan. I don't know what, if anything, he was asked about this. But the -- there are two difficulties. First is we don't know the facts which led this apparent operation to be planned. We have absolutely no idea because it's not part of the indictment, no evidence has been led by the Prosecution nor the Defence about that municipality, who these people were, or what they did, or why any operation was being planned. Secondly, if an operation was planned and never carried out, how is that going to assist the Trial Chamber in assessing anything? So, Your Honours, I maintain my objection to this evidence being led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, if I understand you correctly, wouldn't the point that you wish to make be sufficiently made by merely mentioning Foca as a fact and then -- I shouldn't say as a fact, as an event, and without leading any details about it at all, especially having regard to what Ms. Korner has just reminded us, that, as you yourself have said, the operation planned for Foca was never carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, in the view of the Chamber, Mr. Cvijetic, the witness may be permitted to mention it but without any details whatever because it's totally irrelevant for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will focus on the relevant part, the part from the indictment. I have to ask the witness who the operation was supposed to target and why. We know that the indictment contains the crimes committed also by the paramilitaries against whom that operation would have been carried out. This is how I intend to lead the witness. I'm going to ask him what was supposed to be done against those people. This is the gist of the indictment against Mr. Stanisic, i.e., what he did against certain persons and their actions. As for the reasons why the operation wasn't carried out, I believe that Mr. Andan explored that quite sufficiently, and I do not intend to ask this witness about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're still checking the Andan transcript. At the moment, we can find nothing except a very brief thing saying the operation wasn't carried out and Mr. Orasanin knows about it. But in any event, Your Honour, the problem is this: There is a real divergence between the Prosecution and Defence on the reason why Mr. Stanisic launched action against some paramilitaries but not others, and it's our contention, and that's something we'll be dealing with in the evidence, that the only times that action was launched was when the paramilitaries in question, such as the Yellow Wasps or the Mice, carried out attacks on members of the Serb population. So it's, therefore, important to know, and Your Honours have heard no evidence about this one way or another, who these people were, what they were alleged to have done. And that's the difficulty in allowing the Defence to develop this through a man who knows simply that an operation was planned and abandoned. If that's what he wants to say, he can say it, but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, no more than that. And I would think that what Mr. Cvijetic has just said can be accomplished within the compass of two or three questions at the most. Ms. Korner, what the Chamber -- what I continually bear in mind is that whereas of course we are bound by the fundamental rule of relevance as determined by the indictment, the reality is that we -- the indictment is an artificial delineation of events which occurred in a certain historical time, and there comes a point in which some overlap is inevitable, and this was apparent throughout the case for the Prosecution. So provided Mr. Cvijetic confines himself to, as I said, for what he said, three questions should do it and we move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree. I mean, it's simply the amount of detail that can be gone into that is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cvijetic, when the witness returns, you understand what you're permitted to do. So the usher could escort the witness back to the stand, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, I'll have some very short questions for you and I will invite you short answers. The first one is this: Did you read, did you peruse, Mr. Mico Stanisic's order? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it was an original order. What I mean is that it was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who's the operation supposed to be carried out against?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be carried out in the territory of Foca against criminal and terrorist groups. I still remember the term used, criminal and terrorist groups of paramilitaries in the territory of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that order, did Mr. Stanisic also approve the use of fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a specific reference as far as I can remember -- or, rather, there was one chapter dealing with the application of laws, which is one of the most difficult areas, the use of fire-arms to eliminate and apprehend those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: More specifically, was that part of that order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One paragraph dealt with the use of police authorities highlighting the use of fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in that order were the tasks of your administration also specified and what did they consist of? Again, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were also tasks pertaining to Crime Prevention Administration, the police administration, as well as the administration dealing with logistics. The three administrations were highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm specifically interested in the tasks given to your administration and you personally.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first was to draft an operative plan, to implement that operative plan, to apply authorities and investigative procedures, apprehension, taking people in custody, and filing criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did your tasks also specify the processing of the crimes that were committed by the paramilitaries in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a general application.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And my last question about this topic: The order and the tasks in that order, were they either the same or similar as the order for Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were similarities. The only thing that differed was the use of terminology, specifically "terrorist groups." The term "terrorist groups" was used for the first time because in terms of their activities, in terms of the fact that they were renegade armed groups, that meant that they were terrorists and they should be treated as terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
