utterances.text: In keeping with the previously-given promise, we will not go on. Before we open a document which has just been translated, and it will take a few minutes to upload it, I will have just one more question. After all your visits and after all your inspections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, on this Foca operation, one follow-up question, please. Mr. Orasanin, do you remember the date or the approximate date of that order, of Mr. Stanisic's order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was issued in mid-August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, if you were asked to summarise all your visits across the Republika Srpska and across all the public security stations, would you be able to highlight the main problems in the work of crime prevention services that would be common to all of them, not just individual problems? If you were asked to highlight the most pressing problems that hinder the work of those services, can you just give me a list of the most prominent problems?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first problem was the lack of professional staff, as we have already seen. So the main problem was personnel. When we inspected the area, we realised that another big problem was the fact that those paramilitary groups were not under anybody's control. They were not under the control of either the military or the police. And they were the main cause of the problems in Foca, Zvornik, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And what about the local bodies of authority, were there any hindrances on their part?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the local authorities or, rather, the Crisis Staffs at the beginning effectively controlled even the police. In some towns they even appointed commanders and chiefs of their police stations and that was also a very big problem. Probably the local authorities were in cahoots with some of those local renegade groups. For example, in Brcko, I believe that we were chased away by their snipers. And that was one of the key problems. The issue was how to establish the work of the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, how to establish control over those paramilitary groups in Foca and Zvornik where the police stations were not in control of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now I will ask you about the year 1992. Do you perhaps know or could you be able to assess the percentage of detected and resolved crimes in the territory of the Republika Srpska? You don't have to be very precise but maybe you can give us an approximation. Did your service carry out any analysis in that sense? This a very concrete question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's start with that one, shall we, the basis for which he can give any such opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, you've heard Ms. Korner. Start with last things first. Did your service carry out an analysis of the crimes that were detected and resolved in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is within the purview of our analysis service and the Crime Prevention Administration. All the reports that arrived at our desk were analysed. I personally was not involved in that. In any case, the analysis serves to monitor the work of the security services centres and public security stations. I know that the percentage was very high in our view, especially in the Security Services Centres of Banja Luka and Doboj. The total percentage was over 45, up to 50 per cent of the crimes that were resolved. In peacetime, I know that a percentage of over 40 to 50 per cent is considered a good performance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have received the translation of the document. I would suggest that we take a short break which will allow us to upload it. And after I show the document to the witness, I will have a few questions and that will be the end of my examination. I will have no other questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we would -- would the usual 20-minute break, or should I add an additional five minutes or so?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that a half an hour that we normally take should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will return at the usual time of 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address you briefly before the witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, before the break there was a discussion about the evidence on Foca and the witness Andan, and I understand Ms. Korner hadn't had time to check the transcript, but can I just for the record state that on the 30th of May in relation to Exhibit 1D557, that was Andan's personal diary, he was questioned about the Foca operation at pages 21503, -504. That was on direct. Again on direct, in relation to Exhibit 1D556 -- sorry, 1D566, that's a letter from Prime Minister Djeric, he was questioned about Foca at pages 21545, -547. Finally, on direct, Exhibit -- or not exhibit, it's 65 ter 179D1, an Official Note, and there he's questioned at 21552, -555. And finally, on cross-examination by the Prosecutor on the 1st of June, Andan was questioned about Foca at pages 21697 to -706. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. And of course while Ms. Korner had no personal recollection of this, the Chamber, certainly one of the members, did recall that the witness Andan spoke specifically to the matter of Foca. Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, we will continue where we broke off, but do repeat once more, did you have an opportunity to see it while you were working there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I suppose that in the mean time you were able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here is my question: Does this request, which is reiterated, refer to the -- to entering information in the forms about war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 3, that the nationality of perpetrators or victims need not be entered. Is that in line with what we've explained?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ethnicity was not an issue. It was the same for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There's another statement in the introductory part. Take a look at the date of the minister's first dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a reference to previous dispatches, dated 16 May and 19 July. Those were earlier dispatches about the submission of the forms mentioned here, RZ and RZ1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness is obviously acquainted with this document and he acted pursuant to the orders of the minister, he even took part in the drafting of the forms, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D572, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, you don't know but I still owe something to the Prosecutor, namely whether or not you gave a document to the Defence, so that is made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 65 ter 143D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 36. Let us wait for the technician to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, you said at the beginning that you were transferred from the crime prevention unit to the uniformed police, more specifically, the border police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you give us this document that we see here?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly why you considered it important for us to receive this document. In one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you this document because in the border department there were also some problems with the jurisdiction of the MUP and the military respectively or, more specifically, the military police. The military police assumed the jurisdiction over some things that were -- that should properly have been in our jurisdiction, and there was a problem. The MUP was unable to carry out the assignments that it was legally bound to do. We can see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the latter part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are offices of the border police whose superior I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the end of your previous answer. It was about the overlapping jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is about the interference of military bodies, that is, the military police, in the work of the border police of the MUP, and this report was filed by officers at the border crossing of Zvornik whose superior I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness is here and he brought this document, I will tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours think a document about the border patrol on the 25th of January of 1993 is relevant, I'll leave it up to Your Honours. We would say it's not relevant to anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will amend my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, the date here is indeed 25 January 1993, so let me ask you if these problems with the clash of jurisdictions go back earlier than this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This was from January when the border police became operational, but in November and December of 1992 it was the same, only worse. I found this report and I brought it here as an example, but there were more drastic cases back in August and September. We had to work in accordance with laws and regulations because there was an embargo imposed in Serbia and there were UN observers there, and we insisted that everything should be in line with the regulations, that the military police do their job, and the MUP, their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To whom was this report sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You heard the question, witness.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was sent to the MUP, that is, to the chief of the border department of the MUP of the RS, to have the ministry solve the problem with the military. It's about jurisdiction. The minister should have seen to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, insofar as the witness in your -- in the last exchange, that is, the one before the -- to whom the report was sent, he has explained, he has given viva voce testimony about events prior to January of 1993, so that emphasizes the irrelevance of this particular report. What is -- what may be of assistance is the latter part of his testimony about similar events having occurred in 1992, so this report is of no assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I appreciate the position of the Trial Chamber, and I withdraw my motion to tender this document. Now at least we know the provenance of the document, and I hereby conclude my examination-in-chief. Thank you, Mr. Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, I haven't forgotten the answer that you gave to us yesterday, but for the record at this point I just wish you to confirm that you decline cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, when I spoke to Mr. Cvijetic this morning, he assured me he'd take the rest of the day and tomorrow, or part of it, so -- but I am actually in a position to start. I should say, Your Honours, just so Your Honours know, I will complete my cross-examination tomorrow and we'll be ready for the next witness to start on Thursday. I told Mr. Zecevic last week that I wouldn't be very long, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Orasanin, let's deal with document, shall we. You produced for the Defence these two documents which you told the Court that you didn't have at the time you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And before you were seen in 2004, I believe it was, by an investigator from -- sorry, 2005, by an investigator, he presumably asked you when you were contacted to bring with you any documents you had that might assist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask me to bring any documents. We only agreed about the time of our interview in Sarajevo. That was in our telephone conversation. In any case, I didn't have those documents at the time. Actually, I knew that those documents existed somewhere, but they were not accessible to me in 2004. That is why my 2004 statement doesn't involve those documents which in my mind are authentic and valid. I found those documents only recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'll come on to that. Where did you find those documents now some - what's the date? - 2011, nearly -- well, 18 years or thereabouts after the event? Where did you get the documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the document in the house in the village where my mother lived. Already then in 2004 I knew that some papers, some notes, were lying around somewhere. They were in that house, but I only found them later. There are a lot of papers hanging around there. It is our family house and some of those papers belong to my brothers. That document was produced in 1992. It's an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Orasanin, I'm going to emphasise: If you answer the questions shortly, and they're simple questions, you will be out of here definitely by tomorrow. If you give me long answers like that, you'll be here until the next day. Now, all that required you to say was that you found it at your parents' or your brother's house. That document, one of them at least, in fact both of them, are confidential MUP documents, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are copies. There were three copies of the same document, and that document was the typist's copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it purports -- let's go back -- I'm not interested in the last one. It purports to bear your signature, that's what you told the Court. I've forgotten what number it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I apologise, let's clarify one matter. What is the basis for Ms. Korner's conclusion that the document is confidential? She doesn't -- she hasn't laid sufficient a ground to put this question to the witness. How does she know that the document is confidential?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, actually, I rather thought it was self-evident that a report on an inspection to the minister would not be something that was for publication. However, I will ask that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reports that you did after inspections, those were for the eyes of the minister, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to submit that to our boss, the assistant minister, or the head of the Department for Crime Prevention. As for the rest of the procedure, it was our immediate superior who was in charge of that. And this document is not confidential, and I have kept this copy. The other two copies were sent for further proceedings. They were sent into the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you telling the Court, Mr. Orasanin, that when you prepared these or signed these reports about inspections or any other documents, that they -- you were entitled to give them, for example, to the press?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a special procedure in place for any contacts with the media, and one had to have authority in order to provide information to the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because you couldn't just give internal MUP documents to anybody, could you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document never went to anybody outside of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But are you telling the Court that you were entitled to take home and keep for yourself copies of documents that you had given to the minister or the assistant minister, whoever it might have been?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every employee could keep any copies of any documents to remind them what they did, and that's why I kept this document. But this is either a third or even a fourth copy, and I did not violate any rules. This is not a confidential document. There's no degree of confidentiality attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By confidential, I mean it's internal MUP document. You're not allowed to hand it to anybody outside the MUP, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to check where this leads to. The witness has already answered that this document was not intended for anybody's eyes. He just kept it for himself because he was one of its authors. I don't know how far Ms. Korner is going to go with this line of questioning and what else can be achieved with this line of questioning in addition to what this man has already told us about the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was quite wrong for Mr. Cvijetic to try and give the witness the answer that he wants. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I, too, was wondering how much farther you're going with this, and I'm wondering whether, to what extent, the short answer to your question is that Bosnia has no equivalent of what we would know as the Official Secrets Act.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that's correct, in fact. And we've had other evidence about it but I am pursuing this for a reason that you will, I hope, see in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the document up on the screen, please. I think it's 1D064320, or something like that, at tab 29. Oh, 33D1. Sorry. I don't know what 1D064320 is then. Sorry, can we have the third page in English and the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you sign it if it's just a copy that you kept for your own purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is my copy. I signed it because it's mine. The first and the second copies were signed by Nikola Milanovic, myself, and Ostoja Minic. I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all three of you signed the copy that went up to the assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I just want to know why - this was simply your own personal copy kept at home - you signed it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. There is my name there. It just signifies that this copy is mine, and I'm sure that each of the other two has kept their respective copies in their archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what else have you got at home? I mean, firstly, I'm sorry, before we get on to that, what else did you give to the Defence? What other documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've provided this one, the one that we have just commented upon. It's at tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to know, outside what's in this binder, how many other documents did you give the Defence? Outside what is in here, how many other documents, when you first saw them, whoever you first saw, how many documents did you give them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. He has to answer the question, not you, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just going to say that the witness has already answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first and the second report, tab 29, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Outside those two documents that are in this binder, what other documents did you give the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. You should ask the witness whether he gave anything. Ms. Korner is leading the witness and suggests that he indeed has given other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, there is nothing wrong with the question. Let the witness answer it. Please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Orasanin, for the third time, don't look at Mr. Cvijetic for help or assistance, how many documents outside these two did you give the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You sure?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two documents. The first report and the second report dated the 1st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you have other documents in your home or your parents' home which relate to the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Possibly I have some handwritten notes, for example, an operative plan related to a visit to Foca. I had worked on that personally, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I ask why you kept that particular report or those two particular reports on those two instances and nothing else? What was so particularly important about your inspection on Visegrad, and other places?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special, but that was on the 14th of September. That was my last visit, when I was already in the middle of the preparations for transfer, I was about to be transferred into the border police department, so those were the last events that I participated in before I was transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As an inspector you were obliged to keep a notebook, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not an obligation. However, when we went on our visit, one would always take notes which were then served for our joint report, because all of our reports were joint reports, the one from Doboj, another one from Foca and Cajnice. Those were our joint reports signed by the three of us because all the three of us had been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You did a number of inspections with Mr. Ostoja Minic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he carry a notebook with him on those inspections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he did. It was either him or Milanovic actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he carried one, how come you didn't carry one?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we did the same things. When we were there, we were there all three of us at any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you did some inspections without Mr. Minic. On those occasions did you get somebody else to keep notes of what was said?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all of those cases, there was myself, Milanovic, and Ostoja. We made a team. And we worked together in Banja Luka, Doboj, Brcko, Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As well as Visegrad. Well, in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where is the report that you did on the Doboj visit on the 15th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it exists. This is an earlier report, that's why I don't have it. And this report reflects my thoughts before my transfer. There had already been discussions about me being transferred to another service, and I'm sure that it was submitted to the Crime Prevention Administration, this report from Doboj, and as far as I can remember it is similar to this one. The method of work was the same. And if somebody were to produce that report, you would see that the procedure described in that report is similar to this one, and that procedure relied on the instruction on how to do inspection visits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in a minute. All right, so you have no idea where that report for the 15th of August visit might be?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be with the Crime Prevention Administration of the Republika Srpska MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And in your getting hold of documents, it didn't occur to you to go and try and find that one?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just a coincidence. It was September on the eve of my transfer. I kept this one for that reason. But this is a copy bearing my signature. The first and the second copies were signed by the three of us. That was part of a regular procedure. There's nothing unusual about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue that, although, Mr. Orasanin, it's somewhat curious. Some people might think that you signed simply a copy that you're keeping yourself. However, let's go back to the beginning, shall we. You told the Court that you had been at the Novo Sarajevo Police Station as the assistant commander until such time as the conflict started at the beginning of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that you hadn't actually been working since February of 1992, having declared yourself to be on sick leave from that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, let me explain. I was the chief of the Crime Prevention Department and as of the end of February I was on a sick leave. The day before yesterday I explained that I did come to work every other day and I did because of my obligations and because of the people who were working there. They came from different ethnic backgrounds and I couldn't leave them because we dealt with custody cases every day. That police station had 125 uniformed police officers, 15 inspectors. There was the commander of the police station who was in charge of the uniformed police. And at that time I was in charge of signing custody decisions. I was the only person authorised to do that. I went on a sick leave for some reasons. I can explain, but it will take me two or three minutes to explain why I went on a six leave. The reason was lack of professionalism, the service had been joined by some new people who were in cahoots with criminals, and we all felt the same, not just myself but also the Croatian and Bosniak inspectors. But I couldn't leave them. I came back to work every day in order to deal with the custody cases and also when there were some events taking place, for example, cutting Sarajevo into different parts. And I can even tell you the reason why I went on a sick leave if you want me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, in a moment you can if you want to, but the point that I'm making is you led the Court to believe in your evidence-in-chief that you had been working full time at this Novo Sarajevo Police Station before the events of early April, and that is not correct, is it? You did not tell the Court anything about being on sick leave nor about you being -- coming every other day into the police station.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can find it in my first statement in the audio recording. I've never been in this courtroom before, but I thought that there was no need for me to go over the same things that I already said in 1994. It is true and correct that I was on sick leave. I went on a sick leave because of a commission, and it's a special story. There was a commission at the level of the Ministry of the Interior; it was a governmental commission in charge of investigating a trail of some money and burning of some money and things like that. I wanted to avoid that because I thought it was a way to frame people up. I didn't want to be a member of that commission. That's why I went on sick leave. However, I continued working. I continued co-operating with the operatives who were there. I had to be there. Those operatives, they were of different ethnic backgrounds. Nobody could remand a person in custody if a decision to that effect was not being signed. We had custody cases every day. For example, the killing Petrovic, Pero. And that proves how hard people worked. A criminal was apprehended who had broken into several vehicles, and that person Pero Petrovic and his Bosniak neighbourhood [as interpreted] brought them in, and that Bosniak neighbourhood [as interpreted] was a policeman, and that's why he asked him to help him to get the person to the police station. My operative who was on duty -- I was the one who actually assigned people on duty. That inspector was on duty, and when that event had taken place, he informed me by telephone about a crime that had taken place where the conditions were in place for remanding him in custody, and then I had to come, I had to be there, I had to be present. That's why I had to be present, because I was the only one who had the authority to sign decisions on remanding people in custody. I would come to work every other day. For example, there were individuals whom we would remand in custody two or three times in one month. For example, we would remand them in custody, then we would refer him to the court, and then the court would release him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 63 -- page 63, line 8, the year recorded is 1994. Maybe Ms. Korner could come back to that. Let's clarify the period in question. It must be a typo. I'm sorry, I think that the year has been wrongly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no doubt at all it was 1992 that he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, look, Mr. Orasanin, as I said to you before, I'm asking fairly simple questions. If you disagree with my suggestion that you were on sick leave and therefore were not working at the police station during this period, all you have to say is "you're wrong," instead of this long, long explanation. Now, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner, my intervention was only with regard to the year when he was interviewed by the OTP. It says that it was in 1994, so I kindly asked you to correct that, the time of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have already. I've told -- I've said -- given that it's 2005 in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Orasanin, you told -- as you say, you told the investigator in 2005, and I will read out what you actually said to him at page 4 of the transcript: "Starting from the beginning of February, I was on sick leave, and when the war erupted I was still on sick leave." And my suggestion to you, Mr. Orasanin, is that having been on sick leave, you're in no position to give the Court any description of the events which led up to the beginning of the conflict, and that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg to disagree. Although I was on sick leave, I still performed my duties. I worked. I was present. I was there. So I know about all those events. When the police station was attacked, the day before I had left my car there and then I left. I worked. I performed all of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's deal with this attack on the police station in Novo Sarajevo. It's right, isn't it, that a gang of masked men that evening attacked the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And nobody knows whether those men were Serbs or non-Serbs, because they were masked.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may. Sorry, I should have said it's a question.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group had arrived from the area of Stari Grad, old town. They had arrived into vans. They changed their clothes in the vicinity of the outpatient's clinic. They attacked the police station. They killed some people, and they kidnapped a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Have a look, please, at a report of this incident in Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the OTP binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the OTP binder, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I've been informed that this document has never been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be disclosed because it's a public newspaper, open source, and in any event it would never have become relevant had not the Defence decided to go down the road of the attack on Novo Sarajevo Police Station, which I objected to originally. If there's no further objection, I'm going to ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you read this account at the time? It's a report of -- in the newspaper on the -- it's the 8th of April. Yes, 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And if we come to the relevant part, which is on page 2 in English, attack on the SJB Novo Sarajevo: "A dramatic night followed between Saturday and Sunday after the split of the special task force," pausing there for a moment. Were you aware of the split in the Special Police that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk about it, that the Special Police had split.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "50 masked men conducted an attack on the public security station, and on that occasion policeman Pero Petrovic was killed. And the station was robbed and destroyed." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But I don't know which number of members is correct, 30 or 50 or any other number. I don't think that this information is not correct. I know that they had come in two vans from Stari Grad and that they were headed by a certain Puska and that they were members of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this -- oh, yes, quite. This is what the Serbian MUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I think that the full name of the ring leader be recorded. This witness mentioned it but it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't hear it, but what's the full name of this certain Puska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zakid or Zahir, I'm not sure. This is our intelligence, that he brought them, but whether he ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As the report goes on to say: "The Serbian MUP release an announcement. Basic message - Putsch of Green Berets members of the Muslim part of the MUP state in an announcement that they occupy the building of the ministry and the base of the special task forces Green Berets are accused of attacking the public security station in Novo Sarajevo." And that's the fact, isn't it, that a statement was actually put out by Mico Stanisic to the effect that this attack had been carried out by what were described as Green Berets? That's right, isn't it, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this event with the man who was kidnapped, Lazar Bojanic, immediately after the event. And I said two days ago, concerning the police station and their operations during the absence of the commander, he takes responsibility. And he was even an experienced police officer. They disarmed him when they entered the police station, they took him to the basement, they lined up him and Pero Petrovic, since Pero had processed this person. They broke into the storage, and one of these men pointed a pistol at him. They -- actually, he leaned the pistol against his back. And they made him turn around and face the wall. And the -- he fired the pistol into the heart of Pero Petrovic. He was taken to the Elektrodistribucija where --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, stop, please. I'm not asking you for a full description of what you say happened. I'm merely dealing with the people involved. These people were masked people, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness answered but it wasn't recorded. If this is correct, page 68, line 4: "He was taken to the Elektrodistribucija," and then the witness said who was located there but it wasn't recorded. Why not let the witness say what was located there? Because that's the question [as interpreted] to Ms. Korner's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the headquarters of the Green Berets, a group was there even before this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two days after -- I'm sorry, two days after this event, it's right, isn't it, that the Serbs did attack, and there's no dispute about this, the station and seized it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. That the Serbs attacked the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the -- by the 6th of April, the Bosnian Serb MUP was in possession of Novo Sarajevo Police Station, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of April? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Tintor is, please, Mr. Orasanin? Jovan Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him, but he has nothing to do with Novo Sarajevo. He had contacts in the Vogosca municipality. This is probably a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, it's not a misunderstanding. You know who he is. He was the president -- he was a member of the SDS and president of the Crisis Staff in Vogosca, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you also know a Mr. Danilo Veselinovic? V-e-s-e-l-i-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he worked there. I don't know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if necessary we can play you this intercept, but I'm going to ask you to look at the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is at 10391.08, which is -- oh, sorry, it's Exhibit P1500.08 and tab 2. And can we look, please, in English at page 3, and in B/C/S I think it's page 2. Yes, bottom of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tintor is saying to Mr. Veselinovic: "Now we just need to take what is with the police station Novo Sarajevo." "Oh, that is already seized." "Are you kidding me."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then over the page in English, and B/C/S as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic says "aha." "Has it been seized really?" says Mr. Tintor. And he says, this part: "I mean, they've taken everything up to here, up to this one." Right. Now, do you accept it would appear from that, Mr. Orasanin, that two days after this incident, Novo Sarajevo, the SJB, was in the hands of the Bosnian Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because people didn't work there. The Serbs withdrew after the attack, and it stayed in the hands of the Bosniaks. I never entered the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you didn't because you went off again. You went off to the country somewhere, didn't you, and stayed there until you decided to join the Bosnian MUP in April or May, the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the police station was not controlled by the Serbs. Zeljko Rakic was there who was supposed to conduct an on-site investigation after the murder, and they were unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, so --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from him. I have a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Veselinovic has got it all wrong, has he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1.000 per cent wrong. This is the first time I see it and hear it. This is a disinformation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Between two Serbs talking to each other on the telephone? Two members of the -- high members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment their conversation. I took no interest in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Because you told the investigators that -- and indeed I think you told the Court, you left Sarajevo between the 3rd and 4th of April, "the night when the attack occurred at our police station in Sarajevo," and you went to your country -- you went to a village "with my family and stayed there for about three or four weeks." That's what you told the investigator in 2005. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't have known at all what, if anything, had happened in the SJB in Novo Sarajevo, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was in charge of these things and the inspector to conduct an on-site investigator had the task to do that. And I said that this person was -- if the person had been detained, we would have been duty-bound to process it and forward the file to the prosecutor's office. That's what I know. I was active. I did go to the countryside, but upon my return I spoke to Zeljko and the others and I'm familiar with the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How could you have been active if you were living in the country out of any sort of communication with your police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't active during that period, nor were they, because the police station had been taken and disarmed and they didn't work either. Nobody was active during that period. But when I arrived, I spoke to Inspector Rakic and I learned about all these facts and events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, so you say. So before that you were on sick leave, after the incident you left, and you didn't do anything until May of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before I went on sick leave I was permanently present at the police station with the commander. Alija Kazic was the commander, and we had coffee every morning, and everybody else, until this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, just as a matter of interest, how come your superiors allowed you to stay on sick leave if you were actually there the whole time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained, because I was the only one authorised to sign detention cases --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm asking you how come your superiors at that stage, and this is before April 1992, allowed you allegedly to be on sick leave, when in actual fact you were turning up every day?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they couldn't do it otherwise. The authorisation was linked to my name, and a change would have required a special procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you come to work for Mr. Planojevic? You haven't explained that. Who asked you to come and work?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At some time in early May when I arrive at Pale, I went to the MUP. And Dobro Planojevic was appointed to establish a Crime Prevention Administration. That was after the 4th of April, 1992, at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring to the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking how you came to potter along to Pale in the middle of a conflict, according to you, and ended up working for Planojevic. Did somebody ask you to come there? Were you appointed to come there? What?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I stated all that in my first statement, but I see that my first statement isn't here. I explained that. And I explained to the investigators, too. There were only two options: either to join the army, that was a legal obligation, or join the MUP. And since I'm a professional police officer, that's the only thing I can do, I decided to go there, and that's logical. But there was no third option. And I heard that Minister Stanisic was there and that he was trying to set up an organisational structure, because it was all built from scratch. But it was logical for me to be here, because there was no other option. Or possibly I could have returned to the place where Pero was killed and where my apartment was looted and searched. And it was immediately after the attack on the police station, my apartment was searched twice. Perhaps I should have returned there, but I opted for the other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, of course, you might have had to go and actually get involved in combat if you had gone to the military, mightn't you, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we must leave it there for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I ask one thing. It can be dealt with tomorrow, but, Ms. Korner, at page 67, starting line 19, it's about the attack on the Novo Sarajevo Police Station. You asked a question, particularly the part of it starting at page 21. The witness started giving an account of the event itself but didn't answer the question. Could you put that question again to him and, if possible, get a brief answer from him. But tomorrow will be fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With your indulgence, Mr. Zecevic has asked me to convey a request to the Chamber. He's not here, as you can see. He is arriving Thursday morning. He would like to address the Chamber on Thursday concerning scheduling matters for the remainder of our Defence case and procedural matters which are connected to the scheduling. So he would like the opportunity to address you on the Thursday afternoon. Even if we finish with this witness tomorrow, he would like to address you on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you're on your feet, I was about to ask of the Stanisic team whether, having regard to Ms. Korner's indication that she would be completed by tomorrow, whether you have a witness available for Thursday and Friday, bearing in mind that Monday is a holiday, but you can answer that question tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I say, as I say, I did make it clear to Mr. Zecevic that this witness would be finished fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We take the adjournment to tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
